Since late 2022, she has appeared alongside her father dozens of times at high-profile events (Photo: Reuters) North Korean leader Kim Jong Un's daughter, Kim Ju Ae, is increasingly being viewed as his potential successor, with several defectors believing that she is being prepared to inherit power in the reclusive country. Several North Korean individuals who defected to South Korea were interviewed by the Associated Press; according to them, North Koreans have no role in choosing their future leader, and believe that a third hereditary transfer of power would be publicly accepted by the population. The succession question has gained attention as Kim, 42, has made repeated public appearances with his daughter over the past four years. Although little is known about her, her prominent presence alongside her father at major state events has fuelled speculation that she could eventually lead the country. North Korea has been ruled by three generations of the Kim family since its establishment in 1948. The country's leadership passed from founder Kim Il Sung to his son Kim Jong Il in 1994, and then to Kim Jong Un in 2011. Neither transition was accompanied by any known public resistance. The next succession will determine who governs a nuclear-armed country of around 26 million people, where political freedoms are severely restricted and the state maintains extensive surveillance. Most defectors believe Kim's daughter is his heir 
 Kim Ju Ae is reportedly around 13 years old. Since late 2022, she has appeared alongside her father dozens of times at high-profile events, including weapons tests and military parades. North Korean state media has described her as Kim's “most beloved” and “respected” child. Her prominence has also been highlighted through official imagery, including photographs showing an elderly general kneeling before her and the teenager standing in front of her father. Former NBA star Dennis Rodman was the first to reveal her identity publicly, saying he had held Kim's daughter as a baby during a 2013 visit to Pyongyang. However, doubts remain over whether Kim Ju Ae will eventually take over, largely because she is a woman in a political system where women remain significantly underrepresented in senior positions. According to South Korea's unification ministry, only one of the ruling Workers' Party's 17 department directors is a woman. That position is held by Kim's younger sister, Kim Yo Jong, who is an influential figure in the country's leadership. South Korean officials also believe Kim Jong Un has another, younger child, although the sibling's gender has not been confirmed. Lee Si-young, a North Korean defector who heads Seoul-based Free North Korea Radio, said some of her older contacts in North Korea were unhappy with the prospect of a woman taking power. However, she said members of the Kim family were regarded as “gods reigning over humans”, adding that gender did not matter in determining the country's leadership. Why another hereditary succession may face little resistance 
 Regardless of whether Kim Ju Ae becomes the next leader, observers believe Kim Jong Un is likely to select one of his children to continue the family's rule. They expect such a move to encounter little resistance within North Korea, at least publicly. “North Koreans will passively accept a hereditary succession as something that they should go along with,” Ahn Chan-il, a defector and head of the World Institute for North Korean Studies in Seoul, told AP. The country's previous transitions offer some indication of how a future succession could unfold. Kim Jong Il had spent around two decades as his father's designated successor and worked alongside Kim Il Sung before taking over in 1994, when he was 52. The transition to Kim Jong Un in 2011 was less predictable. At 27, he was considered young and inexperienced by outside observers. He nevertheless consolidated his authority through a series of purges and high-profile executions, including the killing of his powerful uncle, Jang Song Thaek, in 2013. South Korea's intelligence agency has recently assessed that Kim Jong Un is extremely obese and faces a high risk of cardiovascular disease, although it has found no other indications of poor health. The assessment has added to attention surrounding the question of who could eventually succeed him.
